stimulus.text: And it hath accordingly happened that an open resistance to the execution of the laws hath actually taken place in the town of Boston, and the neighbourhood thereof... so much of the charter, granted by their majesties King William and Queen Mary to the inhabitants of the said province of the Massachusetts Bay, in New England... be revoked... and that the council, or court of assistants... shall be composed of such of the inhabitants... as shall be thereunto nominated and appointed by his Majesty...

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — Massachusetts Government Act, 1774 (abridged), public domain.

books.section: A. Colonial Resistance to British Policies in the Aftermath of the French and Indian War
The Sugar Act, the Currency Act, and the Stamp Act

stem: Parliament passed the Coercive Acts in 1774 hoping to isolate Massachusetts from the other colonies. The result was the opposite because...

options.text: Massachusetts immediately declared independence, forcing the others to follow
options.misconception: Massachusetts declared nothing in 1774 — independence was still two years away, and the colonies rallied to Massachusetts rather than following a declaration.

options.text: British troops refused to enforce the acts in Boston
options.misconception: The troops enforced the acts — the port was closed and the government was taken over. The failure was political, not military.

options.text: Other colonists saw the acts as threatening their own liberties
Parliament repealed the acts within weeks of passing them
options.misconception: Parliament never repealed the Coercive Acts — the colonies organized the First Continental Congress to resist them instead.

rationales.C: Background: London meant the acts as an example to frighten the other colonies. Instead, colonists everywhere read them as a warning of what London could do to any colony — and the First Continental Congress was the answer.
rationales.A: No declaration was made in 1774. The colonies rallied to Massachusetts; none of them declared independence.
rationales.B: The troops did enforce the acts. The port closed and the government changed hands — the failure was in the plan, not the soldiers.
rationales.D: Repeal never came. The Coercive Acts stayed, and the Congress was organized to resist them.
rationales.general:
1. Name London's plan. Punish Massachusetts alone, and the other colonies will step back from the troublemakers.
2. Ask how the other colonies read it. Not as Massachusetts' punishment, but as a preview: what London did to Boston, it could do to any of them.
3. See the result. Assemblies condemned the acts, committees organized resistance, and the First Continental Congress met — the isolation failed because the threat was shared.
Remember: an example only frightens people if they think it cannot happen to them — shared danger makes allies, not bystanders.
